title: Legitimate expectation
subtitle: When a public body's own promise becomes a ground of review
objectives: Explain how legitimate expectation developed as a distinct ground of judicial review, and state the GCHQ test for when an expectation arises
Distinguish a procedural legitimate expectation from a substantive one, and explain what each protects if a public body departs from it
Apply the Coughlan/Bibi framework to a new fact pattern to decide whether frustrating an expectation amounts to an abuse of power

leadingAuthorities.citation: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374 (GCHQ)
leadingAuthorities.role: Recognised legitimate expectation as a distinct ground of judicial review, alongside illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety

leadingAuthorities.citation: R v North and East Devon Health Authority, ex p Coughlan [2001] QB 213
leadingAuthorities.role: Leading authority on substantive legitimate expectation and the three-category framework for resolving a broken promise
Confirms a legitimate expectation can arise from a promise made to a group, and shows the remedy where a decision-maker fails to factor it in at all

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often treat legitimate expectation as a synonym for 'this feels unfair'. Where the profile shows application lagging knowledge, this note appears: 'You can define the doctrine — this lesson is about proving the promise was clear enough, and picking the right remedy when it wasn't kept.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the GCHQ and Coughlan tests by name already. The test pool below leans hard on fact patterns — expect to be asked whether a promise was clear and unambiguous, not to recite the doctrine.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush the GCHQ test — the rest of this lesson assumes you can state, unprompted, what makes a representation 'legitimate' in the first place.

overview.hook: In 1993, Pamela Coughlan was told by her health authority, in terms she and her fellow residents were entitled to take literally: Mardon House would be her home for life. Seven years later, the same authority decided to close it. Nothing in the law of contract could help her — there had been no bargain, no consideration, nothing signed. And yet the courts intervened. This lesson is about why a government promise, kept in no contract at all, can still bind the government that made it.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. This is a well-established common law doctrine with no legislative reform pending, though its precise boundaries — especially how far substantive legitimate expectation extends beyond individual, personal promises — continue to be tested and refined case by case.

parts.heading: A ground of review born in a labour dispute
parts.voice: narrative — opens with the case that coined the doctrine before naming it
body: In 1984, without warning or consultation, the government banned trade union membership at GCHQ, the signals intelligence agency, citing national security. The unions didn't argue the ban was irrational, or that the Minister lacked the power to impose it under the prerogative. They argued something narrower and, at the time, novel: staff had for years been consulted before changes to their conditions of employment, and that consistent practice had generated an expectation — a legitimate one — that consultation would happen again.

The House of Lords agreed the unions were right about the law, even though they lost on the facts (national security displaced the duty to consult). Lord Diplock, giving judgment, listed 'legitimate expectation' as a freestanding head of judicial review sitting alongside illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. A promise or a settled practice by a public body, he held, can create a legally protected expectation in the person it was made to or established for — even though no contract exists and no statute requires it.

That is the doctrine's origin point, and it is worth holding onto: legitimate expectation exists to hold public bodies to their own word, not to a general standard of fairness at large. Everything that follows in this lesson turns on how clear that word has to be.

components.definition: An expectation, generated by a public body's clear promise or settled practice, that it will act (or refrain from acting) in a particular way — protected by judicial review even though no contract or statutory right exists.

interaction.prompt: Which case first recognised legitimate expectation as a distinct ground of judicial review?
options: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (GCHQ)
Anisminic v Foreign Compensation Commission
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Lord Diplock's speech in GCHQ is where legitimate expectation joins illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety as a named ground of review.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: That's Anisminic — the ouster-clause case. The case that names legitimate expectation as a ground of review is GCHQ, decided on a union consultation dispute in 1984-85.

parts.heading: Two different promises, two different remedies
parts.voice: structural — the reference part students will return to before an exam
body: Not every broken promise is treated the same way, and this is the distinction the exam will test hardest. A legitimate expectation can be procedural — an expectation of being consulted, heard, or given notice before a decision is made — or substantive — an expectation of receiving an actual outcome or benefit.

Procedural expectations are the easier case: if a public body promised consultation and then decides without it, the decision is usually unlawful unless there's an overriding public interest reason not to consult (as in GCHQ itself). Substantive expectations are harder, because upholding one means holding a public body to the outcome it promised, not just the process — which risks a court fettering a body's ability to change policy in the public interest. The courts allow substantive expectations to be enforced, but only where frustrating them would amount to an abuse of power — a much higher bar, developed fully in Coughlan (Part 3).

A rough rule of thumb: ask what, exactly, was promised. 'We will consult you' generates a procedural expectation. 'You will get X' or 'this will be your home for life' generates a substantive one — and substantive claims need the stronger justification the next two parts build.

components.label: Procedural vs substantive legitimate expectation
points: Procedural expectation — a promise of process (consultation, a hearing, notice) before a decision; breach is usually unlawful unless an overriding public interest justifies departing from it
Substantive expectation — a promise of outcome (a benefit, status or result); breach is unlawful only where frustrating it amounts to an abuse of power
The GCHQ test for either kind: the promise or practice must be clear, unambiguous and devoid of relevant qualification, and relied on by an identifiable person or group
A general policy statement, or a promise made without authority to make it, will usually fail the 'clear and unambiguous' threshold before the analysis even reaches procedural/substantive

components.caseName: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (GCHQ)
components.factsShort: Staff at GCHQ had long been consulted on changes to employment conditions; the government banned union membership with no consultation, citing national security.
components.ratioShort: A settled practice of consultation can generate a legitimate expectation of consultation; but a sufficiently weighty public interest (here, national security) can override it.

expanded.facts: The Prime Minister, exercising a prerogative power over the civil service, instructed that staff at GCHQ could no longer belong to trade unions, effective immediately and without any prior consultation with the unions — departing from years of established practice of consulting on changes to employment terms.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords held that the settled practice of consultation had generated a legitimate expectation that consultation would occur before further changes. On the facts, however, the government was entitled to depart from that expectation because national security considerations justified acting without consultation — a public interest the courts would not second-guess on the evidence before them.
expanded.significance: GCHQ does two things at once: it creates the doctrine, and it immediately shows its limit. An expectation, however clearly established, can still be lawfully overridden by a sufficiently weighty countervailing public interest. The union lost the battle but the case is remembered for the ground of review it built.

interaction.prompt: Put these events from the GCHQ dispute in the order they happened.
items: Government establishes a settled practice of consulting GCHQ staff on changes to conditions
Government bans trade union membership at GCHQ with no prior consultation
Unions argue a legitimate expectation of consultation has been breached
House of Lords accepts the expectation existed but holds national security justified overriding it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the shape of the whole case: the expectation is built by practice, broken by the ban, argued in court — and then lawfully overridden on the facts. The doctrine survives the loss.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the practice has to be established first, before the ban that breaks it, before the legal argument, before the national security justification is weighed.

parts.heading: Coughlan: when breaking a promise is an abuse of power
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the full story of the case that carries the lesson
body: Pamela Coughlan was severely disabled in a road accident. In 1993, her health authority moved her into Mardon House, a purpose-built NHS facility, and told her and the other residents in unambiguous terms that it would be their home for life. In 1998, facing budget pressure, the authority decided to close Mardon House and move residents elsewhere, arguing that changing healthcare needs across the district justified reallocating the facility.

The Court of Appeal held the closure was unlawful. Because the promise was so specific, made to a small and identifiable group, and had been relied on in an obviously life-shaping way, holding the authority to a general policy-change justification was not enough — frustrating the promise had to be shown to be proportionate to a legitimate public aim, and on the facts it wasn't. The health authority hadn't offered evidence that closing Mardon House specifically (rather than making savings elsewhere) was necessary.

Coughlan is remembered for the three-category framework it set out for handling any legitimate expectation case, and it's this structure — not just the sympathetic facts — that the exam will test: category (a), a simple policy that can be changed at will if there's no specific promise to an individual; category (b), a procedural expectation, reviewed for fairness; and category (c), a substantive expectation so specific and relied-upon that resiling from it is an abuse of power unless justified.

components.label: The Coughlan three categories
points: (a) Macro-policy — the body is simply changing a general policy; the court asks only whether the policy change is rational (ordinary Wednesbury review)
(b) Procedural — a promise of a fair procedure before a decision is made; the court enforces the promised procedure unless overridden by a sufficient public interest

(c) Substantive, specific promise — a promise so clear and specific, to a person or small group, that resiling from it is scrutinised for proportionality; frustrating it is unlawful unless justified as a proportionate response to a legitimate aim

components.caseName: R v North and East Devon Health Authority, ex p Coughlan
components.factsShort: A health authority promised severely disabled residents that a care home would be their 'home for life', then decided to close it for budgetary and policy reasons.
components.ratioShort: A clear, specific promise relied on by an identifiable group can generate a substantive legitimate expectation; resiling from it is unlawful unless the authority shows an overriding public interest that justifies the proportionality of doing so.

expanded.facts: Miss Coughlan and other residents of Mardon House had been given an explicit assurance, at the time they were moved there, that it would be their home for life. Years later the health authority, restructuring services across the area, decided to close the facility. Miss Coughlan sought judicial review, arguing the promise created a substantive legitimate expectation the authority could not simply override.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that where a public body makes a clear and specific promise to an individual or small group, and that promise is relied upon, the body cannot resile from it merely by showing a rational policy reason. The question is whether frustrating the expectation is so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power — assessed by weighing the authority's reasons for change against the promise's specificity and the reliance placed on it.
expanded.significance: Coughlan is the foundational case for substantive legitimate expectation in English law. It confirms that judicial review can, in a narrow category of cases, protect an actual outcome and not merely a fair process — and it supplies the three-category structure examiners expect students to apply, not just recite.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Coughlan, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
interaction.passage: The health authority argued that changing service needs justified closing Mardon House as a matter of policy. The court accepted that policy could change, but held that where a specific and unambiguous promise has been made to a person, and relied upon, the authority may only resile from it where to do so is a proportionate response to a legitimate public interest — otherwise, frustrating the promise is an abuse of power. On the evidence here, no such justification had been shown.
interaction.ratioSentence: The court accepted that policy could change, but held that where a specific and unambiguous promise has been made to a person, and relied upon, the authority may only resile from it where to do so is a proportionate response to a legitimate public interest — otherwise, frustrating the promise is an abuse of power.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the core holding: policy can still change, but a specific, relied-upon promise raises the bar to proportionality review, not ordinary rationality review.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the sentence that states the actual test the court applies to a broken promise, not the sentence that just describes the health authority's argument or the outcome on the facts.

parts.heading: Does the promise have to be personal? Bibi and group expectations
parts.voice: case-narrative — continues the storytelling register, extends the doctrine
body: Coughlan involved a small, named group of residents. A natural question follows: does legitimate expectation only protect promises made to identifiable individuals, or can a local authority's promise to a wider class of people count too? Bibi answers that question.

Newham LBC had wrongly treated Mrs Bibi and Mr Al-Nashed as intentionally homeless, and as part of resolving that error the council told them — and others in the same position — that they would be provided with secure accommodation. When the council later came to allocate housing, it treated this as simply one factor among many in a general homelessness policy, rather than as a legitimate expectation it had to reckon with directly.

The Court of Appeal held that a legitimate expectation had indeed arisen from the promise, even though it had been made to a defined class of people rather than a single individual — and, crucially, that the council's error wasn't refusing to honour the promise outright, but failing to recognise it existed as a legally relevant factor at all. The remedy wasn't to order the council to give the exact housing promised (the court can't dictate the outcome of a genuinely discretionary decision) — it was to quash the flawed decision and require the council to reconsider, this time treating the promise as the weighty, specific factor it was.

components.factsShort: A council promised secure housing to a group of claimants it had wrongly classified as intentionally homeless, then failed to treat that promise as a relevant factor when later allocating housing.
components.ratioShort: A legitimate expectation can arise from a promise to a defined group, not only a named individual; the remedy for ignoring it is reconsideration that gives it proper weight, not an order compelling the exact outcome promised.

expanded.facts: Newham LBC had unlawfully assessed the claimants as intentionally homeless. In correcting course, council officers assured them of secure accommodation. When housing was later allocated, the council treated its earlier assurance as just one input into a broader discretionary policy, without directly grappling with the fact that a specific promise had been made.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal confirmed that a legitimate expectation is not confined to promises made to a single named person — a promise to an ascertainable class can found one too. Because the council had never squarely addressed the promise's existence and weight in its later decision, that decision was flawed and had to be retaken with the expectation properly factored in.
expanded.significance: Bibi widens legitimate expectation beyond the Coughlan facts (one individual, one home) and clarifies the appropriate remedy: courts will rarely order the specific substantive outcome promised, because that would usurp a public body's discretion — instead they quash and remit, requiring the decision to be retaken with the promise given due weight.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume the remedy in a successful legitimate expectation claim is always an order forcing the public body to deliver exactly what was promised.
components.whyItsWrong: Courts are cautious about dictating the outcome of a discretionary decision that Parliament gave to the public body, not to the judiciary. Even where a legitimate expectation is breached, the usual remedy is to quash the decision and require reconsideration that gives the expectation appropriate weight — as in Bibi. A court will only go further and effectively enforce the specific promised outcome in the clearest cases, closer to Coughlan's facts, where reconsideration would be a foregone conclusion.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario most closely mirrors Bibi rather than Coughlan?
interaction.scenarioA: A council tells a named tenant her specific flat will remain hers for life after a refurbishment programme, then sells the block regardless.
interaction.scenarioB: A department tells everyone who applied under a now-closed grant scheme that applications submitted before the closure date will be assessed under the old rules, then applies the new, stricter rules to all applicants without addressing the earlier assurance.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. B involves a promise to a defined class (all pre-closure applicants) that the decision-maker then simply overlooks — that's Bibi's structure. A is a single, highly specific personal promise about one flat, which is closer to Coughlan.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at who the promise was made to. A promise to one named person about one specific thing sits closer to Coughlan; a promise to a defined group, later ignored rather than expressly justified, is Bibi's pattern.

parts.heading: Applying the framework end to end
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the test items will probe
body: Pull the doctrine together into a workable sequence. First, was there a promise or settled practice at all, and was it clear, unambiguous and devoid of relevant qualification — a vague policy aspiration won't do. Second, who was it made to: a named individual, a small identifiable group, or the world at large through general policy? Third, is it procedural (a promise about process) or substantive (a promise about outcome)? Fourth, applying the right standard for that category, has the public body shown a sufficient justification for departing from it?

The examiner's favourite trap is skipping straight to 'is this unfair?' without first establishing that a sufficiently clear promise existed. If the alleged promise is really just a general statement of policy — 'we aim to consult stakeholders on major decisions' — there is no legitimate expectation to breach in the first place, however disappointed the claimant is.

The second favourite trap is treating any breach of a substantive expectation as automatically unlawful. It isn't — Coughlan itself makes clear that a sufficiently weighty, evidenced public interest can justify resiling from even a specific, individual promise, exactly as national security justified overriding the expectation in GCHQ.

components.title: Legitimate expectation: a decision path
components.description: A flowchart for classifying and resolving a legitimate expectation claim.

nodes.label: Is there a clear, unambiguous promise or settled practice, devoid of relevant qualification?
No → no legitimate expectation arises; review, if any, proceeds on ordinary rationality grounds
Yes → who was it made to: an individual/small group, or the public via general policy?
Promise concerns process → procedural expectation: enforce unless an overriding public interest justifies departing from it (GCHQ)
Promise concerns outcome → substantive expectation: ask whether frustrating it is a proportionate response to a legitimate aim (Coughlan)
Promise made to a defined class → check the decision-maker actually weighed it, not just noted it (Bibi)

components.textAlternative: First ask whether a clear, unambiguous promise or settled practice exists, with no relevant qualification. If not, there is no legitimate expectation and review proceeds on ordinary rationality grounds. If a promise exists, identify who it was made to. If it promises a process, it is a procedural expectation, enforceable unless an overriding public interest justifies departing from it, as in GCHQ. If it promises an outcome, it is a substantive expectation, assessed by asking whether frustrating it is a proportionate response to a legitimate aim, as in Coughlan. Where the promise was made to a defined class rather than one individual, also check that the decision-maker actually weighed the promise as a specific factor, not merely noted its existence, as required by Bibi.

interaction.prompt: A university tells a named PhD student, in writing, that her funding will continue for a fifth year 'given the exceptional circumstances of her case'. The following year, under new budget rules, the university withdraws all fifth-year funding across the board without addressing her individual letter. Which is the strongest ground?
options: Substantive legitimate expectation — a specific, individual promise was made and relied on, and the university has not shown its general policy change justifies overriding this particular assurance
No legitimate expectation — funding decisions are always non-justiciable
Procedural legitimate expectation only — she was merely entitled to be consulted before the decision
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. This is Coughlan territory: a clear, individual promise of an outcome, and a general policy justification that hasn't grappled with that specific promise at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Funding decisions by universities discharging public functions are reviewable, and the promise here is about an outcome (continued funding), not merely a process — so this is a substantive expectation claim, closest to Coughlan.

testPool.prompt: Which case first recognised legitimate expectation as a ground of judicial review?
acceptableAnswers: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service
CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service
testPool.modelAnswer: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374 (the GCHQ case), in Lord Diplock's speech.

testPool.prompt: Is a general, vague statement of policy aspiration ('we aim to consult widely') normally enough to found a legitimate expectation?
options: No — the promise must be clear, unambiguous and devoid of relevant qualification
Yes — any public statement of intent is sufficient

testPool.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the Coughlan three categories?
options: Macro-policy, reviewed for rationality only
Procedural expectation, reviewed for fairness
Substantive expectation, reviewed for proportionality
Statutory expectation, automatically binding regardless of context
testPool.trapExplanation: There is no 'statutory expectation' category in Coughlan, and nothing in this doctrine is 'automatically binding regardless of context' — even the strongest substantive expectations can be lawfully overridden by a sufficient public interest justification.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps a court takes when analysing a legitimate expectation claim.
items: Identify whether a clear, unambiguous promise or settled practice exists
Identify who the promise was made to
Classify the promise as procedural or substantive
Apply the appropriate justification standard to any departure from it

testPool.prompt: Legitimate expectation, unlike the other three grounds of review named in GCHQ, is chiefly a creature of which source of law?
options: Common law developed case by case, not a statute
The Human Rights Act 1998
The Senior Courts Act 1981

testPool.prompt: In the passage below from Bibi, highlight the sentence stating the ratio on remedy.
testPool.passage: The council had made a clear promise of accommodation to an identifiable class of claimants. Because the later decision never squarely addressed that promise as a relevant and weighty factor, it was flawed. Where a legitimate expectation has not been properly taken into account, the appropriate remedy is ordinarily to quash the decision and require reconsideration giving the expectation due weight, rather than for the court to dictate the substantive outcome itself.
testPool.ratioSentence: Where a legitimate expectation has not been properly taken into account, the appropriate remedy is ordinarily to quash the decision and require reconsideration giving the expectation due weight, rather than for the court to dictate the substantive outcome itself.

testPool.prompt: A prison tells an inmate, by letter, that he will be transferred to open conditions once he completes a specific rehabilitation course. He completes it, but the prison then refuses the transfer, citing an unrelated, generic risk-assessment policy that pre-dated the letter. What is the strongest argument?
options: Substantive legitimate expectation — the promise was specific and relied on, and a pre-existing generic policy is unlikely, without more, to justify overriding it
No expectation arises because prison decisions are never reviewable
Only a procedural expectation arises, entitling him to a hearing but nothing more
testPool.explanation: This mirrors Coughlan: a specific, individual promise about an outcome, relied on by completing the course, and a justification that doesn't engage with the specific promise at all.

testPool.prompt: A minister announces in a press release that 'the government intends to keep the current visa fee structure for the foreseeable future'. Six months later, fees are increased in the Budget. Does a visa applicant have a strong legitimate expectation claim?
options: No — this is a general policy statement, not a clear and unambiguous promise to an identifiable person or group
Yes — any public statement by a minister automatically binds future policy
Yes, but only as a procedural expectation of consultation
testPool.explanation: 'Intends... for the foreseeable future' is qualified and general — it fails the GCHQ threshold before the procedural/substantive question is even reached. This is the trap the lesson flags directly.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most strongly pushes this scenario towards a Coughlan-style substantive expectation.
testPool.scenarioText: A local authority runs a general consultation on care home closures, gathering views from all residents affected. Separately, it had told Mr Osei in writing, by name, that his specific room would remain his 'for as long as he needs it'. The authority later closes the whole facility.
tappableSpans: told Mr Osei in writing, by name
testPool.correctSpan: told Mr Osei in writing, by name
testPool.explanation: The general consultation is neutral background; it's the specific, individual, written promise to Mr Osei that supplies the clear and unambiguous representation Coughlan requires.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely mirrors GCHQ's outcome, where an expectation existed but was lawfully overridden?
testPool.scenarioA: A council has consulted residents before every past planning decision in a ward; it skips consultation once, citing an urgent structural safety risk to a school building that needs immediate closure.
testPool.scenarioB: A council promises a named family rehousing within three months after finding their flat unsafe, then simply forgets and offers no justification at all when the deadline passes.
testPool.explanation: A mirrors GCHQ: a settled practice generates a procedural expectation, but a weighty, evidenced public interest (safety) justifies departing from it. B has no justification offered at all, so it isn't an example of lawful override.

testPool.prompt: In Bibi, did the Court of Appeal order the council to provide the exact housing originally promised?
options: No — it quashed the decision and required reconsideration giving the promise due weight
Yes — the court directly ordered the specific accommodation to be provided

testPool.prompt: A hospice tells a small group of long-term patients, individually and in writing, that a specific specialist unit will remain open for their care for as long as they need it. Two years later, facing a funding shortfall across the wider trust, the trust decides to close the unit as part of a general cost-cutting review that does not mention the earlier letters. Analyse whether the patients have a legitimate expectation claim.
factsToOrder: Specific, individual written promises were made to a small, identifiable group
The promise concerned an outcome (the unit remaining open), not merely a process
The later decision was justified only by a general cost-cutting review
The general review did not address or weigh the specific earlier promises
The patients relied on the promise as long-term, dependent patients

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the trust's decision to close the unit unlawfully frustrates a substantive legitimate expectation.
modelAnswer.rule: A clear, unambiguous promise of an outcome, made to an identifiable person or small group and relied on, generates a substantive legitimate expectation; frustrating it is unlawful unless the public body shows the departure is a proportionate response to a legitimate public interest (Coughlan).
modelAnswer.application: The promises here are specific, individual and concern an outcome, closely mirroring Coughlan's facts. The trust's justification is a general cost-cutting review that never engages with the specific promises at all — it shows no reasoning about why this unit, specifically, must close rather than savings being found elsewhere, which is exactly the gap that was fatal to the health authority's case in Coughlan.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The patients have a strong substantive legitimate expectation claim; absent a more specific, evidenced justification addressing the promises directly, the closure decision is likely unlawful and open to review, though a court is more likely to quash and require reconsideration than to compel the unit's continued operation outright.

testPool.prompt: Why does the substantive category in Coughlan require proportionality review rather than mere rationality review?
options: Because rationality review sets too high a bar for public bodies to ever meet

Because holding a body to an actual outcome, rather than just a fair process, risks improperly restricting its ability to change policy — proportionality review balances that risk against the promise's specificity and reliance
Because proportionality review is required automatically whenever a claimant is an individual rather than a company
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers focus on the claimant's identity or on rationality being 'too easy' — neither is the real reasoning. The heightened scrutiny exists because enforcing an outcome, not just a process, is a bigger intrusion into a public body's discretion, so the justification for departing from it needs to be correspondingly stronger.

testPool.prompt: Order the events of the Coughlan litigation.
items: Residents are assured Mardon House will be their home for life
The health authority decides to close Mardon House for budgetary and policy reasons
Miss Coughlan seeks judicial review of the closure decision
The Court of Appeal holds the closure is unlawful without a stronger, more specific justification

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is skipping the threshold question — was there a sufficiently clear, unambiguous promise at all — and jumping straight to arguing about fairness. No clear promise, no legitimate expectation, however disappointed the claimant is.
